### Moment 1
What you did: I look at Ambrose, slow, and say, "Ambrose. Children won't wake, and the clock's ticking too fast. You know this tower. Is it the clock doing it, or is it something else? Tell me what you know, and I'll pay for it fair if it costs."
Why: I can't sleep, and the hearths in the children's houses have gone cold, which sits wrong with me. Ambrose keeps the clock, so he's the first one to ask. If he wants payment I'll count it out, because I won't owe him for it.
What happened: You look at Ambrose, slow, over the workbench of tiny cogs, and tell him plainly: the children won't wake, and the clock is ticking too fast. He knows this tower. Is it the clock doing it, or something else? Whatever he knows, you'll pay for it fair if it costs.

Ambrose: He taps the bench in time with the chains, once, twice, and his spectacles slip down from his bald head. "No coin, young sir. No coin for this." A creak of a breath. "My grandfather told me: once in a hundred years, the Wumbleby clock tries to strike thirteen at midnight. On the thirteenth stroke a road opens out of the world, and whatever's waiting in town goes down it, taking what it came for. Ninety-nine years and some months, young sir."

Ambrose: "Fast for three days now. Since the peddler came. I can't slow it." He points a stained finger at the ceiling and the ladder. "The Great Gear, up in the gearloft. Jam something stout and iron in its teeth before midnight, and she'll never strike thirteen. Not wood. Iron. I've no iron bar here, I've looked. But every hearth in town has a poker." He rubs a knee. "And I can't climb that ladder any more."

Overhead the chains twitch, and the tick comes down through the floor into your boots. The old man is watching your face, waiting.

### Moment 2
What you did: I nod slow at Ambrose and say, "Iron in the teeth. Fair's fair, I'll fetch it." I head south to the Lopsided Square to get a poker from the nearest hearth, and I'll pay the house its price in buttons rather than owe a favour.
Why: Ambrose wants no coin, and I'll not leave it unpaid in my own head, so I'll stop the clock and settle for the iron fair. The children are cold and sleeping, and there's little time before midnight, so I'm going for a poker now.
What happened: You nod slow at old Ambrose, say that iron in the teeth is fair, and that you'll fetch it. Then you go out by the south door, down into the Lopsided Square.

The cobbles slope under your boots and the fog hangs thick about the lamps. Every window round the square is dark. Pip Pumbleton sits on the fountain's rim with a cricket bat across her knees, and the old woman in her shawls dozes by her cart. Dilly Quickstep stands near, the lamplighter's pole in hand. Overhead the clock ticks loud enough to feel in your teeth.

Crooked Lane winds on south into the fog, and the Pumbletons' leaning house waits to the west.
What changed: you went from The Tock Tower to The Lopsided Square; you met Mags Ragwort, Pip Pumbleton.
What you were told: Dilly Quickstep says: "Easy as winking, chum. Marigold's not going down Crooked Lane alone, and neither are we. Hobb, you lead the way with your lantern, and I'll keep the pole high so nothing sneaks past us in the fog."
What happened: Dilly gave Pip a wink and a pat on the shoulder, said they would not let Marigold go down Crooked Lane alone, and went out of the square by the south road with the lamplighter's pole held high.
What happened: Somewhere close, a soft sing-song voice is calling "Toys! Toys for the little ones!" and a tray of tin things hums along.

### Moment 3
What you did: I turn to Mister Tibbersnatch, slow, and say, "You. Peddler. Pip's brother's shadow, and the other children's. Where are they? Hand them back, and if it costs, I'll pay fair." I keep my big frame between him and the south road, so he can't slip off into the fog.
Why: The peddler came three days ago and the clock started running fast, so he's the one holding the shadows, and Ambrose's iron won't help the children if they stay stolen. I'll hear his price first and count it out, because I won't owe anyone for it, and then I'll fetch the poker before midnight.
What happened: You turn, slow as a door swinging, until you face the tall man in the striped stovepipe hat, and you set your big frame between him and the south road. "You. Peddler," you say. "Pip's brother's shadow, and the other children's. Where are they? Hand them back, and if it costs, I'll pay fair."

The toys on his tray hum on. His grin doesn't shift by a hair, and his long, many-jointed fingers drum a slow tune on the tray's edge.

Mister Tibbersnatch: "Oh my dear, my dumpling, so grim and so loud, you frighten the toys and you won't fool the crowd. The shadows are safe in a jar, snug and tight, and they travel with me when the clock strikes midnight. But a bargain's a bargain, and I never renege: I'd give you the lot for a thing I can't gain. I've tunes in a box and tunes in a bell, but never a whistle worn-in and well."

He tips his hat to you, as polite as a Sunday. Above the rooftops the Tock Tower ticks on, loud enough to hear in your teeth, and the fog waits at the foot of the hill.

What do you do?
What changed: you met Mister Tibbersnatch.

### Moment 4
What you did: I look at the peddler, slow, and say, "A whistle, worn-in and well. I've none on me. Tell me plain, Tibbersnatch: any whistle will do, or must it be a certain one? Mags, you buy odds and ends. Have you got one on your cart?" I step toward Mags's cart and keep the peddler in the corner of my eye.
Why: The peddler wants a worn-in whistle, and a bargain I can pay is better than a fight I might lose. Mags deals in odds and ends, so she may have one, and I'll count out buttons for it fair. Then it's the poker for the clock before midnight.
What happened: You look at the peddler, slow, and tell him a whistle, worn-in and well, is something you haven't got on you. Plainly, you ask: will any whistle do, or must it be a certain one?

Tibbersnatch: The grin stays exactly where it is, though the long fingers tap a slow rhythm on the tray of humming toys. "Not any whistle, my dear, nor one that's shiny and new. It must be tin, and old, and loved for fifty years, with a tune worn soft the whole way through. Bring me that, and the jar is yours, a bargain fair and true."

You step over to Mags's cart by the dry fountain, keeping the stovepipe hat in the corner of your eye, and ask whether she has a whistle among her odds and ends. Duchess the donkey blinks at you sleepily.

Mags: She sucks her teeth. "Rags an' bones, petal. Bottles an' bits. I sell nothing, an' I've no whistle for you."

Pip sits on the fountain's rim with her cricket bat, glaring down the hill. Above the rooftops the clock ticks loud enough to feel in your teeth.

### Moment 5
What you did: I turn from Mags and look at Pip, slow, and say, "Pip. Tin whistle, old, loved fifty years. Children on Crooked Lane were whispering of one. Know whose it is?" If she doesn't, I head south down Crooked Lane to find them, and I'll pay buttons for the whistle if it's owned, fair and counted.
Why: The peddler will trade the shadows for a worn-in tin whistle, and the talk says Crooked Lane children know of one. I'll find it and pay for it fair so I owe no one, then fetch the poker for the clock before midnight.
What happened: You turn from Mags's cart and look at Pip, slow. She sits on the fountain's rim with her cricket bat across her knees, and the gas lamps catch the mud on her boots.

Hobb: "Pip. Tin whistle, old, loved fifty years. Children on Crooked Lane were whispering of one. Know whose it is?"

Her grip tightens on the bat.

Pip: "Yes, I know whose it is. It's old Mr. Tock's, up in the clock tower. He plays it every sunset, and he's done it for years. The peddler wants it, doesn't he? He took Tod's shadow, and seven other kids' too, and I want them back before midnight. Will you help, or are you another grown-up who just stands there?"

The clock above the square ticks loud enough to feel in your teeth. Pip is waiting for your answer.
